groups.title: Terrain illumination vs NASA polar illumination maps
groups.explanation: NASA Goddard (Mazarico et al. 2011, PGDA product 69) published the share of time any part of the solar disc is visible over a full 18.6-year lunar nutation cycle, and the share of time the Earth is visible (any part of its disc). The maps are computed as seen from the surface, so this check uses observer height 0 m; our app uses 2 m (shown in the notes). We run our own horizon model on LOLA terrain at the centre of the same map pixel (85°S map at 60 m where it covers the site, else the 65°S map at 240 m), 2020-01-01 + 18.6 years, every 1 h. Here we use the available LOLA grid closest to the map: 80 m + 240 m for the 60 m map, 240 m for the 240 m map (its pixel centres are the 240 m DEM points); the app adds 20 m within 5 km. The 60 m product label names LDEM_85S_060M; we have the 2021 adjusted DEM instead. To isolate that difference, the 'Same DEM' rows run the same model on LDEM_75S_120M, the DEM named by the 120 m map AVGVISIB_75S_120M_201608, at that map's pixel centres (sites at 75–90°S). PDS serves that DEM as version 2.0 of 2017-06-15; the map label is dated 2016-09-15, so the map used an earlier version of the same grid. Beyond the 75°S edge of that grid the rays use LOLA 240 m. The 60 m map is also run on LDEM_75S_60M V2.0, the same 60 m grid as the LDEM_85S_060M its label names ('Same 60 m DEM' rows, pixel and 7×7 patch). For that map these rows are the scored Sun checks; the Sun rows on our 80 m DEM are kept as a reference, because they measure the DEM difference (D-023). Every site also has a matched 7×7-pixel median absolute difference check. AREA registration describes pixel cells; the illumination model is evaluated at their centres, not averaged over each cell. No registration offset is fitted to the reference values.

groups.title: Earth eclipses the Sun vs the NASA GSFC eclipse catalogue
groups.explanation: During a lunar eclipse the Earth disc passes over the Sun disc as seen from the Moon. The app counts the limb-darkened Sun disc flux that is above the terrain and outside the Earth disc. The Earth disc includes an opaque air layer by the Danjon rule (radius × 1.01), the rule of the NASA GSFC catalogue. We check the geometry against the catalogue contact times. The catalogue gives contacts for the whole Moon (P1 = the penumbra first touches the lunar disc, U1..U4 the umbra, P4 = the Moon leaves the penumbra). We find the same instants as the first and last of 20000 points on the lunar sphere whose Sun the Earth disc touches (P) or covers fully (U). A single site enters the shadow later than P1 and leaves it before P4, so for a site we check that its times fall inside the catalogue window. We compare in Dynamical Time: the catalogue printed UT with a Delta T predicted in 2009 (75–76 s); the real TDB − UTC is 69.2 s. Tolerance 30 s. The terrain checks above (PGDA 69, Barker) do not apply eclipses.

groups.title: Regolith surface temperature vs Diviner and Apollo
groups.explanation: The task names thermal conditions for equipment. We compute the regolith surface temperature with the 1D heat conduction model of Hayne et al. (2017, JGR Planets): density and conductivity grow with depth, conductivity and heat capacity depend on temperature. We check the model against the reference values in Table A2 of the paper (albedo rising with the incidence angle, Eq. A8): Diviner equatorial temperatures and the Apollo 15/17 heat flow probes. At the polar sites the model takes our hourly solar flux behind the terrain horizon (2024–2027, SPICE) on the tilted ground and gives the 2027 minimum and maximum. There the albedo is 0.12 at every incidence angle, as in the polar terrain model of Hayne et al. (2021, Nature Astronomy, Methods). We chose it after the first run: with Eq. A8 the Sun at 1–2° gives albedo 0.7–0.8, and the sites came out 20–71 K colder than the Diviner polar product. We compare with that product (Paige et al. 2010) at its own scale: the slope of its ~0.5 km triangle and the horizon of LOLA 240 m, the LOLA grid closest to that mesh. We chose the 240 m horizon after a run on the 20 m site terrain: there a 20 m crest hides the Sun at some sites (de Gerlache rim GR1: Sun seen 25 % of hours on 20 m, 54 % on 240 m), which a 0.5 km mesh cannot resolve. On Shackleton rim the 240 m grid flattens the crest and hides the Sun instead. Both models add light and infrared from the sunlit slopes around the site. In ours each azimuth of the horizon is a slope that faces the site, with view factor sin² of its horizon angle. It adds 0–2.2 W/m² on average (IM-1 the most): up to 3 K in the annual mean at 2 cm, about 1 K in the maximum. It is the ground, not the lander.
